episode_title: Tap Into Your Power with Theresa Lear Levine

real_qa.q: What is EFT tapping and how does it differ from talk therapy in treating stress and limiting beliefs?
real_qa.r: EFT is basically acupuncture without the needles combined with talking about what's bothering you. When you tap on different points on your face and body while discussing what's stressful, it immediately sends a signal to your amygdala, which controls your fight or flight response, and calms it down. The body gets the message that it's safe while you're thinking about the stressful thing—the opposite of what normally happens even with talk therapy.
real_qa.requete: EFT tapping acupuncture without needles amygdala

real_qa.q: How can ADHD brains be reframed as an asset rather than a disorder in entrepreneurship and creative work?
real_qa.r: ADHD brains see connections, patterns, possibilities, and problems before anyone else spots them—it's a gift. ADHD brains are wired for interest, novelty, and urgency, and when something lights them up they can hyper-focus like nobody else. Entrepreneurship rewards that because you get to build your schedule around your own energy. However, the flip side is the gap between insight and action, and many successful ADHD people are exhausted from compensating and masking behind the scenes.
real_qa.requete: ADHD brain entrepreneurship gift pattern recognition

real_qa.q: What is the relationship between self-trust, keeping small promises to yourself, and building a new identity?
real_qa.r: Self-trust gets built in the tiny promises you make and keep—every time you follow through, like setting the alarm for Pilates, you're casting a vote for a new identity. The identity needs to show up before the change happens. When you break these promises, most people go into shame, but instead it's important to get curious about what part of you didn't want to follow through, because that data helps you understand yourself better and make different choices.
real_qa.requete: self-trust tiny promises identity casting vote

real_qa.q: How did writing Theresa Lear Levine's book 'Becoming More Me' change when she shifted from masculine hustle energy to pleasure and ease?
real_qa.r: The first time she tried to write it using masculine energy with spreadsheets and word counts aimed at three months of 15-minute daily sessions, it was awful and she hated it. After doing EFT tapping and releasing the project, she came back a year later after collecting information from people on podcasts and speaking engagements. She then wrote it through the lens of pleasure, ease, and abundance—writing while sipping coffee on a deck in Cape Cod during family vacation, lighting candles, and surrounding herself with the right atmosphere.
real_qa.requete: Becoming More Me Theresa Lear Levine pleasure ease masculine energy

real_qa.q: What is the 'Finish What You Start' program and how does it help people rehearse their new identity?
real_qa.r: Finish What You Start is a seven-minute daily practice that Theresa created to help people rehearse who they're becoming, the same way an athlete or Olympian does before competition or winning a gold medal. Following through starts to feel more normal instead of forced, because the system can be turned off when we feel like we're just pushing through with masculine hustle energy.
real_qa.requete: Finish What You Start seven minute practice rehearse identity

guest.titre: Best-selling Author, Keynote Speaker, and EFT Tapping Master
guest.bio_context: Theresa Lear Levine is a best-selling author and EFT tapping master who specializes in helping women stop living on autopilot and reconnect with their authentic selves. She was previously a fitness and nutrition coach and discovered that EFT (Emotional Freedom Technique) and hypnotherapy were transformative tools for creating deep personal shifts beyond intellectual knowledge. She is an ADHD entrepreneur with four sons, several of whom have also been diagnosed with ADHD and autism, and she leverages her own neurodivergent experience in her coaching work.

real_quote: I had a big belief that my productivity equaled my worth. And so rest didn't feel like rest. It felt like danger.
